correctness.rationale: Exact conditional binomial law and Pareto rescaling give an integral with a min(1,v) domination valid precisely for 0<alpha<1. Its limit is Gamma(1-alpha)(1-z)^alpha, justifying the rare-mark Poisson limit with all independence steps explicit. Exact word/split counts give the length threshold and log correction. At the subcritical cutoff no short catalysis is possible, hence no all-short RAF; the published diffuse-kernel Theorem 8 supplies global RAF existence. The program passed finite exact-formula and quadrature tests. No simulation is used to infer an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The inspected source establishes global RAF existence and single-molecule catalysis, not the sharp internal molecular-length window and discrete-stable count, nor their universal every-RAF length obstruction. General compound Poisson, Sibuya laws and heavy-tail asymptotics are acknowledged as known. Hordijk–Steel and other primary results use different catalysis regimes or measure reaction counts or minimum ambient sizes. Best-knowledge originality with stated priority risks, not a uniqueness certificate.
residual_risks: Unindexed standard heavy-tail triangular-array or RAF-depth literature may contain an equivalent specialization; literature absence alone cannot prove uniqueness.
An inaccessible or only partially inspected treatment of size thresholds in polymer RAFs may strengthen an older result to imply a component of this result.
The derived sharp cutoff is for all potential short catalytic incidences; it is deliberately not claimed to equal the minimum RAF molecular length.

value.rationale: Addresses a mathematically motivated RAF structural gap in the recent heavy-tailed catalyst model: below a sharp logarithmically corrected fraction of ambient length, there is no catalytic incidence at all, even though RAFs exist globally; at onset, rare active catalysts have a non-Gaussian discrete-stable burst law. Provides precise testable benchmarking of molecule-length-dependent autocatalysis, not just an arbitrary numerical slice.
